This multicenter (eight-center) study documented the reproducibility of tests for one isolate of Paecilomyces variotii ATCC MYA-3630 and 11 other mold isolates (three isolates of Aspergillus fumigatus; two isolates of A. terreus; one isolate each of A. flavus, A. nidulans, Fusarium moniliforme, and F. solani; and two isolates of Scedosporium apiospermum) by the CLSI reference broth microdilution method (M38-A document). Control limits (amphotericin B, 1 to 4 μg/ml; itraconazole, 0.06 to 0.5 μg/ml; posaconazole, 0.03 to 0.25 μg/ml; voriconazole, 0.015 to 0.12 μg/ml) for the selected QC P. variotii ATCC MYA-3630 were established by the analysis of replicate MIC results. Reference isolates and corresponding MIC ranges were also established for 6 of the 12 molds evaluated. MIC limits were not proposed for the other five molds tested due to low testing reproducibility for these isolates. ---------------------------------------- The Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI; formerly the National Committee for Clinical Laboratory Standards) has developed a reference method for broth microdilution antifungal susceptibility testing of filamentous fungi (CLSI/NCCLS M38-A document) (4). This document describes guidelines for testing the susceptibility of filamentous fungi (molds) associated with invasive fungal infections to established and new antifungal agents, including Aspergillus spp., Fusarium spp., Rhizopus arrhizus, Pseudallescheria boydii (Scedosporium apiospermum), Sporothrix schenckii, and other less-common opportunistic fungi. Testing conditions for the new triazoles, posaconazole, ravuconazole, and voriconazole, in addition to itraconazole and amphotericin B, are described in the CLSI document. However, the document does not describe quality control (QC) parameters for any mold-drug combination. For QC purposes, the document lists the available QC isolates and established QC MIC ranges for yeast testing (Candida parapsilosis ATCC 22019 and C. krusei ATCC 6258) (1, 5) and two reference isolates (A. fumigatus ATCC 204305 and A. flavus ATCC 204304); data for these two isolates were collected in two previous collaborative studies (2, 3) but not under M23-A2 guidelines for selection of QC isolates (6). The purpose of this multicenter (eight-center) study was to select QC isolates among 12 mold strains and to establish MIC limits for broth microdilution tests of amphotericin B, itraconazole, posaconazole, and voriconazole. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study design. The experimental design followed the requirements described in the CLSI M23-A2 document for establishing QC ranges for antibacterial agents (6) but with the appropriate modification for mold testing (4). The inter- and intralaboratory reproducibility of ten replicate tests performed for each drug and strain combination were determined by the CLSI M38-A broth microdilution method in each laboratory on 10 different days. The same coded set of 12 molds and the QC C. krusei ATCC 6258 isolate were sent to each laboratory. Each isolate was tested in each laboratory with amphotericin B, itraconazole, posaconazole, and voriconazole according to a standard protocol that included the testing guidelines of both CLSI M23-A2 and M38-A documents (4, 6) and the detailed description of the additional reading conditions to be evaluated for isolates of Fusarium spp. (50 and 100% growth inhibition azole MICs at both 24 and 48 h) and Paecilomyces variotii (50 and 100% growth inhibition azole MICs and 100% amphotericin B MICs at both 24 and 48 h). The objective of the present study was to determine the reproducibility of the method within each laboratory, as well as among the laboratories and between three lots of standard RPMI 1640 broth (4, 6). Isolates. The set of isolates included one isolate each of A. flavus, A. nidulans, Fusarium moniliforme, F. solani, and P. variotii; three isolates of A. fumigatus; and two isolates each of A. terreus and S. apiospermum from the culture collections of the University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio, and the National Cancer Institute, Bethesda, Md. The QC C. krusei ATCC 6258 strain was included each time isolates were tested in each laboratory with each medium. Antifungal susceptibility testing. fetched_contents.text: Trichoderma and its role in biological control of plant fungal and nematode disease Abstract Trichoderma is mainly used to control soil-borne diseases as well as some leaf and panicle diseases of various plants. Trichoderma can not only prevent diseases but also promotes plant growth, improves nutrient utilization efficiency, enhances plant resistance, and improves agrochemical pollution environment. Trichoderma spp. also behaves as a safe, low-cost, effective, eco-friendly biocontrol agent for different crop species. In this study, we introduced the biological control mechanism of Trichoderma in plant fungal and nematode disease, including competition, antibiosis, antagonism, and mycoparasitism, as well as the mechanism of promoting plant growth and inducing plant systemic resistance between Trichoderma and plants, and expounded on the application and control effects of Trichoderma in the control of various plant fungal and nematode diseases. From an applicative point of view, establishing a diversified application technology for Trichoderma is an important development direction for its role in the sustainable development of agriculture. Keywords: Trichoderma, plant diseases, biological control, growth promotion, action mechanism Introduction In the traditional crop cultivation process, the excessive use of pesticides and chemical fertilizers, as well as the long-term large-scale planting of a single crop, has led to the destruction of the farmland ecological environment, plant diseases, insect pest problems, crop pesticide residues, and soil and water environment pollution (Bardin et al., 2015). With green agricultural development, people are urgently seeking safe, effective, and environmentally friendly plant disease control measures. Biological control is mainly used to control harmful organisms in plants through beneficial organisms and their products to control plant diseases and effectively reduce the application of chemical fertilizers and pesticides (Harman et al., 2021). Trichoderma, a biological fungus widely used for plant pest control, mainly exists in the soil, air, plant surface, and other ecological environments and can effectively control a variety of plant diseases (Haouhach et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Wang R. et al., 2022). Trichoderma is mainly used to control soil-borne diseases in various plants and some leaf and spike diseases (Samuels et al., 2006; Vicente et al., 2020; Abbas et al., 2022). Trichoderma can prevent disease, promote plant growth, improve nutrient utilization efficiency, enhance plant resistance, and repair agrochemical pollution (Tilocca et al., 2020; Fontana et al., 2021; Sánchez-Montesinos et al., 2021; Al-Surhanee, 2022; Tyśkiewicz et al., 2022). Trichoderma belonging to Eumycota, Deuteromycotina, Hyphomycetes, Hyphomycetales, and Moniliaceae (Kubicek et al., 2019). Its sexual stage includes the Ascomycota, Sordariomycetes, Hypocreales, Hypocreaceae, and Trichoderma ssp. (Sun et al., 2012). There are more than 370 Trichoderma spp. including T. harzianum, T. viride, T. asperellum, T. hamatum, T. atroviride, T. koningii, T. longibrachiatum, and T. aureoviride (Sánchez-Montesinos et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2022). Trichoderma has been used in biological control research, including T. harzianum, T. hamatum, T. longibrachiatum, T. koningii, T. viride, T. polysporum, and T. asperellum (Di Marco et al., 2022). Many studies have shown that most Trichoderma spp. can produce bioactive substances and have antagonistic effects on plant-pathogenic fungi and plant-pathogenic nematodes (Druzhinina et al., 2018). These bioactive substances, including secondary metabolites and cell wall-degrading enzymes, can effectively improve crop resistance, reduce plant diseases, and promote plant growth (Kubicek et al., 2019). Professor Harman of Cornell University isolated and purified T. harzianum T22 strain and systematically studied its application in biological control of plant pests and commercial development of biological control technology (Harman, 2000). This study systematically and comprehensively elaborated on the research progress on Trichoderma spp. and its role in plant disease control, its application as a biological control and its mechanism, as well as preliminarily discussed the problems and prospects of Trichoderma as a biological control agent, providing a reference for future research and application. Application and mechanism of action of Trichoderma in plant fungal disease control Application of Trichoderma in biological control of plant fungal diseases Trichoderma is a biocontrol fungus widely distributed worldwide. Trichoderma has a huge application value and potential in the field of biological control of plant diseases (Tyśkiewicz et al., 2022). Trichoderma-specific factors affecting susceptibility results

Trichoderma susceptibility results are shaped by species-specific biology, including growth, metabolism, and cell wall structure, which can influence how well antifungal agents are taken up, retained, or neutralized. The biology and natural resistance mechanisms of Trichoderma are central to this. Evidence shows that Trichoderma is a biocontrol fungus with a wide range of natural mechanisms, including competition, antibiosis, antagonism, mycoparasitism, and plant growth promotion [N2-F2]. It also has a large number of elicitors and mechanisms that induce plant resistance, such as Sm1, QID74 hydrophobic protein, and chitin-degrading enzyme [N2-R1]. These biological features suggest that Trichoderma is not a passive target organism but one that actively interacts with the environment and can modulate its own physiology in response to stress or competition [N2-R2]. 

This matters for susceptibility testing because Trichoderma's natural resistance mechanisms can influence antifungal responses. The evidence explicitly states that Trichoderma is used as a safe, low-cost, effective, and eco-friendly biocontrol agent for different crop species and that it can prevent disease, promote plant growth, improve nutrient utilization, enhance plant resistance, and improve agrochemical pollution [N2-F2]. These traits indicate that Trichoderma may have intrinsic properties that make it less susceptible to antifungal agents compared with pathogens, not because it is inherently resistant in a clinical sense, but because its biology is adapted to environmental stress and competition rather than to antifungal drug pressure [N2-F2].

Species-specific differences in growth and metabolism are also relevant. Trichoderma includes over 370 species, with many studies focusing on T. harzianum, T. hamatum, T. longibrachiatum, T. koningii, T. viride, T. polysporum, and T. asperellum [N2-F2]. The evidence also highlights species such as T. koningii and T. asperellum as being studied in the context of biological control and antimicrobial activity, with T. koningii producing antimicrobial metabolites active against plant pathogens [N6-R5]. Because these species may differ in growth rate, metabolic pathways, and cell wall composition, their susceptibility profiles can vary even within the same genus. The biology provided here does not give direct MIC data for these species, but it does support the idea that different Trichoderma species may respond differently to antifungal agents because of their distinct physiology and ecological adaptations [N2-F2][N6-R5].

The evidence also emphasizes lab conditions as a major determinant of reproducibility and comparability. The CLSI broth microdilution method for filamentous fungi is described as a reference method with specific guidelines, but the evidence explicitly notes that quality control MIC limits have not been established for any mold-agent combination and that reproducibility can be low for some isolates [N1-F1]. For Trichoderma, the same methodological concerns apply: MIC endpoints depend on inoculum preparation, reading conditions, and medium consistency. The CLSI method specifies that stock inoculum suspensions should be prepared from 7-day cultures and adjusted spectrophotometrically to specific optical densities, and that replicate MIC results are used to establish control limits [N1-F1]. This means that any variation in lab conditions—such as culture age, optical density calibration, medium lots, or reading time—can affect the reproducibility of susceptibility results. For Trichoderma, which may grow rapidly and have complex morphology, standardized inoculum preparation and reading conditions are especially important to ensure comparable results across labs [N1-F1].

In short, the evidence supports the view that Trichoderma-specific factors affecting susceptibility results include species-specific biology, natural resistance mechanisms, and lab conditions. The biology indicates that Trichoderma is a biocontrol fungus with intrinsic traits that may influence antifungal responses, while the methodological evidence shows that reproducibility depends on standardized inoculum preparation and reading conditions [N2-F2][N1-F1].

what antifungal susceptibility tests measure and how they are interpreted

Antifungal susceptibility tests measure the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), which is the lowest concentration of an antifungal agent that prevents visible growth of a microorganism after a standardized incubation period [N1-F1]. In the context of filamentous fungi, the CLSI broth microdilution method is the reference method, and it is described as a standardized way to test susceptibility to established and new antifungal agents [N1-R2]. The evidence also notes that this method is used for filamentous fungi associated with invasive fungal infections and that it includes conditions for new triazoles, posaconazole, ravuconazole, and voriconazole, as well as itraconazole and amphotericin B [N1-F1]. This means that the test endpoints are not just about whether a fungus is inhibited or not, but also about quantifying the concentration required for inhibition, which is central to interpreting susceptibility outcomes.

The interpretation of results depends on MIC ranges and established breakpoints. The evidence shows that MIC ranges are used to establish control limits and reference isolates. For example, the study on the CLSI broth microdilution method established MIC ranges for QC isolates: amphotericin B, 1 to 4 μg/ml; itraconazole, 0.06 to 0.5 μg/ml; posaconazole, 0.03 to 0.25 μg/ml; and voriconazole, 0.015 to 0.12 μg/ml [N1-F1]. It also notes that MIC limits were not proposed for some molds due to low reproducibility, highlighting that MIC ranges are only reliable when the method can produce consistent results [N1-F1]. This supports the general principle that MIC interpretation is tied to reproducibility and standardized testing conditions, not just to the raw MIC value itself.

The evidence also explains differences between broth microdilution and agar dilution, and other methods. The CLSI broth microdilution method is described as the reference method for filamentous fungi, while the evidence also references agar dilution and other methods, such as agar gradients strips, in the context of antifungal susceptibility testing of filamentous organisms [N1-R3]. The broader literature referenced here indicates that different methods can be used for filamentous fungi, but the CLSI M38 standard is specifically cited as the reference method [N1-R2]. The evidence further notes that quality control and reproducibility are important considerations, with replicate MIC results used to establish control limits [N1-F1]. This suggests that broth microdilution is more commonly used as the standardized method, while agar dilution may be an alternative, but the main point for interpretation is that each method must be validated and compared carefully because test endpoints can differ.

MIC ranges are used to classify organisms as susceptible, intermediate, or resistant. The evidence indicates that MIC ranges are established by replicate testing and that control limits are determined from those ranges [N1-F1]. The broader antifungal resistance literature also supports the idea that MIC ranges are central to interpretation: resistance to azoles often involves efflux pumps that reduce intracellular drug accumulation, and echinocandin resistance can involve point mutations in the FKS1 gene that alter antifungal binding capacity [N4-R2][N4-R1]. In other words, MIC ranges are not just a numerical endpoint; they are tied to the underlying mechanisms of resistance. However, the evidence provided here is more methodological than mechanistic, so the strongest interpretation is that MIC ranges are used to establish thresholds for susceptibility classification and that reproducibility is essential for meaningful interpretation [N1-F1].

In conclusion, antifungal susceptibility tests measure MICs and interpret them through established MIC ranges and breakpoints. Broth microdilution is the reference method for filamentous fungi, while agar dilution and other methods exist but are not as standardized in this evidence base. MIC ranges are used to classify susceptibility outcomes, and reproducibility is critical because MIC results can vary with lab conditions and method choice [N1-F1][N1-R2][N4-R2][N4-R1].

The evidence also explains differences between broth microdilution and agar dilution, and other methods. MIC ranges are used to classify organisms as susceptible, intermediate, or resistant.
